conventions.convention: The finite nonempty index sets identify fixed conditions i, batches j nested within i, and repeats k starting at 1; each repeat count m_ij is a positive integer. Crossed day and operator effects require a different model.

All batch and repeat effects are jointly independent, square-integrable real random variables on one probability space, with zero means and common batch and repeat variances. Either variance may be zero; Gaussianity is not assumed.

Repeatability concerns the declared short-term conditions; the batch variance describes only the named nested factor. A working random-effects model alone does not justify design-based extrapolation or establish empirical stability.

The calibration example stipulates exact deterministic responses for stable reference quantities 0, 5, and 10 on two days. The pooled affine line minimizes equally weighted squared vertical residuals over all six readings, on the declared calibration range [0,10].

load_bearing.statement: The nested batch measurement model is Y_ijk = μ + τ_i + B_ij + ε_ijk, with fixed real μ and τ_i and jointly independent, centered, square-integrable batch and repeat effects having common finite variances. The replicate mean averages the m_ij readings within one batch.
Under the stated finite nested model, Cov(Y_ijk,Y_ijℓ) = σ_B² for distinct repeats k and ℓ within a batch, and Var(Ȳ_ij·) = σ_B² + σ_ε²/m_ij for every batch. No Gaussian assumption is needed.

published_dependencies.used_for: Total probability mass one, used with expectation as integration to evaluate constants and obtain first-moment bounds.
The measurable-map meaning of real random variables on the common probability space.
Joint independence of the batch and repeat families; independence is assumed rather than inferred from indices.
Expectation as a Lebesgue integral and the finite expectation convention for integrable real variables.
Variance as the expected centered square and covariance as the expected centered product for square-integrable variables.
Linearity for the finite integrable sums in the covariance and replicate-mean variance expansions.
Its integrable case, applied with identity functions to distinct independent components, makes each cross-product expectation the product of two zero means.
